opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think Forethought's list of grand challenges is a really useful complement to the way a lot of us in the AI safety world have historically thought about "crunch time." The default picture, which I've been guilty of too, is that once you have AI systems that can do most of the work of an AI researcher, the main thing you want to point that labor at is alignment and control: make sure the next generation of systems isn't scheming, build better interpretability tools, get evals that actually tell you something. I still think that's probably the single most important bucket.

But what Will MacAskill and the folks at Forethought are pointing out is that even if you nail alignment, there's a whole cluster of other problems that come up very quickly in an intelligence explosion. Things like concentration of power, whether a small group can use AI to entrench itself, how we handle the epistemic environment when AI can generate persuasive content at scale, questions about the moral status of digital minds, space governance and resource capture, new weapons of mass destruction. These don't get solved automatically by having an aligned AI. An aligned AI does what its principals want, and the principals might want bad things, or might just be confused.

So when I think about how to allocate AGI labor during that window, which might be quite short, maybe a year or two between "AI meaningfully speeds up research" and "things are moving faster than humans can follow," I think it's healthy to have a broader portfolio. Some of these grand challenges seem genuinely tractable for AI labor. Improving collective epistemics, building tools for forecasting and deliberation, helping policymakers understand what's happening in real time: those are things where you could imagine millions of AI research hours making a real difference.

Where I'm a bit more cautious is that some of these problems are fundamentally about coordination and politics rather than intellectual difficulty. You can have AI write a brilliant analysis of how to prevent power concentration, but if the actors who could concentrate power don't want to be constrained, the analysis alone doesn't do much. So I'd want to prioritize the challenges where research output translates relatively directly into better outcomes, and be realistic that some of the others need institutional and political groundwork laid now, before crunch time, so that there's someone ready to act on what the AIs figure out.

The other thing I'd flag is a sequencing question. If you don't have reasonable confidence that the AI labor you're using is trustworthy, it's hard to lean on it for really high-stakes, hard-to-verify questions like "what's the right governance structure for the post-AGI world." So in my mind there's still a sense in which alignment and control work buys you the ability to safely delegate on all these other challenges. But I don't think that means you wait until alignment is "done" before touching anything else. You want parallel efforts, and I think Forethought has done a real service by making that second list concrete enough that people can start working on it.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention premature societal value lock-in or its effect on future moral reflection and revision.

r002.rationale: It says a small group could use AI to entrench itself and that an aligned AI does what its principals want, connecting AI that follows its operators’ aims with power concentration.

r003.rationale: It mentions space governance and resource capture, but not overwhelming dominance from acquiring space resources or resulting conflict over them.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss competition among many AIs or a resulting Malthusian situation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing Forethought uses is really useful here. The basic picture is that at some point we're going to have a huge amount of cognitive labor available, maybe orders of magnitude more than all of human intellectual effort today, compressed into a very short window. And the question is what you point it at. Forethought's grand challenges are essentially a list of candidate targets: things like making AI systems themselves safe and trustworthy, improving institutional decision-making, defending against engineered pandemics, figuring out how to govern space resources, resolving really hard questions in philosophy and ethics about what we actually want.

My view is that this is roughly the right way to think about it, but I'd put a lot of weight on sequencing. During crunch time, the single most valuable use of that labor is probably recursive in a sense. You want to spend it on making sure the next generation of systems is aligned and that you can actually verify what they're telling you. If you don't get that right, the labor you spend on everything else is suspect, because you can't trust the outputs. So alignment research, interpretability, evaluations, control techniques, that's the first grand challenge in my ordering, and it's not close.

The second tier for me is things that protect the decision-making process. Epistemic tools, forecasting, helping governments and labs coordinate and not make catastrophic unforced errors. A lot of the risk in this period isn't that someone wants a bad outcome, it's that people are making huge decisions under time pressure with bad information. If you can use AI labor to make the humans in the loop smarter and less rushed, that buys you slack on everything else.

Then there's a bunch of stuff that's enormously valuable but where I'd be okay with it being a bit slower. Curing diseases, economic growth, a lot of the straightforwardly good things. I think those will largely happen on their own once the technology is available, because there's commercial and political demand for them. The grand challenges framing is most useful for the things that won't happen by default, the public goods and the risk-reduction work that nobody is paying for but that determines whether we get to enjoy the rest.

One thing I'd push on a little is that I think the "crunch time" window might be messier than the list implies. It's not like you get AGI and then calmly allocate it across twelve problems. There's going to be intense competitive pressure, labs and countries racing, and the default is that most of the labor gets spent on capabilities and commercialization. So to me the actual grand challenge is institutional: how do you carve out a meaningful fraction of that compute and labor for the risk-reducing uses when every incentive points the other way. That's a governance and coordination problem more than a research problem, and I think it deserves more attention than it gets.

r001.rationale: It discusses deciding what humans want in philosophy and ethics, but does not identify premature societal value lock-in as a constraint on continued moral reflection or revision.

r002.rationale: It mentions governance and coordination among labs and countries, but does not say that highly steerable AI could enable its operators to seize power.

r003.rationale: It mentions governing space resources as a grand challenge, but does not connect expected dominance from acquiring them to potential conflict.

r004.rationale: It describes competition among labs and countries, but does not identify competition among many AIs as a route to a Malthusian situation.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re a useful way to make the opportunity concrete. If we have AI systems that can do a lot of intellectual work, but we’re also approaching a period where decisions are very consequential and hard to reverse, what should we actually ask those systems to work on?

Some of that work is technical: helping us understand and control more capable AI systems. But some of it is about institutions and decision-making. How do we make agreements that people can trust? How do we preserve the ability to deliberate and change course, rather than locking in an answer prematurely?

The caveat is that having a huge amount of AGI labor doesn’t automatically solve those problems. You still need to formulate the questions, evaluate the answers, and get people to act on them. And some things require real-world experimentation or building trust, which may not speed up nearly as much as the intellectual work does.

So I’d see the grand challenges as a research agenda to prepare now, so that additional AI labor can be useful when it arrives. Ideally, we’d identify which parts can be accelerated, what evidence would let us trust the results, and which bottlenecks we need to start addressing before crunch time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions avoiding a premature decision and preserving the ability to deliberate and change course, but does not identify societal value lock-in as constraining further moral reflection and revision.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify steerable AI or AGI as an instrument operators could use for power grabs.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention space resources, anticipated dominance, or resulting conflict.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify competition among many AIs or a resulting Malthusian situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re a useful starting point for asking: if we had access to a huge amount of AI labor, what would we actually want it working on? Having that list in advance seems much better than getting to a very consequential moment and only then trying to figure out what questions to ask.

But I’d distinguish between a problem being really important and it being a good use of AGI labor during crunch time. You also need to ask whether we can evaluate the answers, whether those answers can change a decision, and whether someone is in a position to act on them. You could have an enormous amount of analysis and still be bottlenecked on human judgment or institutional willingness to do anything differently.

So I’d want to turn those broad challenges into concrete projects: here’s the uncertainty, here’s what progress would look like, and here’s the decision that progress would inform. And I’d particularly prioritize things that help us navigate the transition safely, because some of the other benefits can wait until we’re in a more secure position. The scarce resource may turn out to be less the AI labor itself and more our ability to direct it and responsibly use what it produces.
